Thankfully this doesn't appear to actually block anything; it'll produce error output when typing, but the code functions just fine. It's also strangely constrainted, as it only appears when **typing** new characters to the affected line; that is: the error won't appear if saving, backspacing/deleting, or even undoing. This feels more like GDScript territory, so I'll remove myself from assignment

I had a quick look, issue still exists with the reproducer.

From core's perspective, everything is correct - something is accessing a `String` keyed `Dictionary` with `NIL` keys. 
The culprit is `_guess_expression_type` (`gdscript_editor.cpp:2060`). It appears to be indexing the dictionary at hand to understand the type of the return value. I don't think accessing the _actual_ value to do reflection is a great idea, but that's outside the scope of this issue to discuss. 

Anyway, if I'm understanding it right, `_guess_expression_type(c, subscript->index, index)` (`gdscript_editor.cpp:2053`) does something incorrectly, and returns a `NIL` value where it should have returned `STRING`. This is where I'm stopping. Someone who understands this code should have a look. cc @vnen @HolonProduction

The idea here isn't to do reflection, but to have auto completion working in a dynamically typed environment. If we want to continue support for this feature there is no other way than to try calling `get` with potentially invalid keys (the Nil results from `s` not having a reduced value).

I stand by my comment https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/104757#issuecomment-2763273385. `get` should fail silently for typed dictionaries and use `r_valid` to signal errors, like it does for all other variants (as far as I'm aware).

If that is no option for some reason, we can try guarding the calls with `Variant.has_key` (if that fails silently?). 

We might be able to prevent this branch from running if the variable has no validly sourced value (NIL is just a default), similar to `ExpressionNode` which has a `reduced` flag besides `reduced_value`. That would still lead to printed errors if the user makes a mistake (e.g. we properly get a string value from the index used by the user, but the user tries to index an incompatible dictionary), so without a silently failing check there is no real solution.

> The idea here isn't to do reflection, but to have auto completion working in a dynamically typed environment. If we want to continue support for this feature there is no other way than to try calling get with potentially invalid keys (the Nil results from s not having a reduced value).

Thanks for explaining. I think it should be possible to deduce, without using the value of `s`, that values of `dict` getters always yield `int` values (by reflecting the type, rather than the value, of `dict`). I'm not sure how feasible this in our current codebase though, so let me apologize in advance if I'm ignorant about this :) Probably best discussed some other time.

> I stand by my comment [#104757 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/104757#issuecomment-2763273385). `get` should fail silently for typed dictionaries and use `r_valid` to signal errors, like it does for all other variants (as far as I'm aware).

This is a thought worth discussing, but I don't think `Dictionary` is unique in this regard. `Array` for example also `typed.validate` for `.find`, so you'll get the same kind of error. Perhaps we should bring it into the appropriate meetings (Core and GDScript)?

> I think it should be possible to deduce, without using the value of `s`, that values of `dict` getters always yield `int` values (by reflecting the type, rather than the value, of `dict`).

That is implemented, but it seems to happen after attempting the dynamic lookup: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/ee121ef80e36865ac9d5c55ab2ec419f48ef6954/modules/gdscript/gdscript_editor.cpp#L2200-L2208

Might be worth to reevaluate that location, it's probably from a time were type hints were a thing, but couldn't be generic, so the static type was inferior. As of now, the dynamic inferred type is inferior if we know the static one. And I'd argue if something is typed as `Array` or `Dictionary` without generics it's fine (if not more correct) to make no assumptions about the content.

> `Array` for example also `typed.validate` for `.find`, so you'll get the same kind of error

I don't think Array ever gets to `find` when using `Variant.get`. Take this example:

```gdscript
var a: Array[String] = ["1", "2", "3"]

func test():
	var o = Object.new()
	var c = "Test"
	a[c]. # Same code path runs, Variant.get does not error but r_valid = false
	a[null]. # Same code path runs, Variant.get does not error but r_valid = false
	o[null]. # Same code path runs, Variant.get does not error but r_valid = false
```

All those lines call to `Variant.get` when doing code completion. Everytime `r_valid` is `false` but no errors are printed, even though the keys are clearly invalid. Might very well be different when using specific methods on the types, but that's how `Variant.get` behaves at the moment. (It's a bit stupid that core methods like this are largely undocumented, but for me when using it, I read a parameter like `r_valid` as "this method fails silently".)

As for a quick fix for the blocker. Would be nice to know whether `Variant.has_key` is safe to use with invalid keys.

> I don't think Array ever gets to `find` when using `Variant.get`. Take this example:
> 
> var a: Array[String] = ["1", "2", "3"]
> 
> func test():
> 	var o = Object.new()

> 	a[null]. # Same code path runs, Variant.get does not error but r_valid = false
> 	o[null]. # Same code path runs, Variant.get does not error but r_valid = false

I meant more from a Core perspective, than a code completion perspective :)
If you're suggesting to make `getptr` not complain on incorrect types, this would be a change to core behavior. We'd likely need to adjust all other read-only functions (like `.find` of `Array`) to not complain in a similar way, to stay consistent.

> As for a quick fix for the blocker. Would be nice to know whether `Variant.has_key` is safe to use with invalid keys.

I think it would complain (it seems to defer to `Dictionary::has`), but I can't say for sure without testing.
It would be possible to check for `dictionary.get_key_type` before keying the `dict`, but that might be a patchwork solution. Personally, I'd prefer your suggestion above, doing static inference before dynamic inference, if possible.

> I meant more from a Core perspective

Fair 👍, no clue what's going on internally, just saying the method behaves differently than I'd expect without documentation.

> It would be possible to check for `dictionary.get_key_type` before keying the dict

We only have a `Variant` and I'd rather not add special cases for different variant types there. If there is a unified Variant API to get something by key/index, there should be a unified way to test the validity of such a key/index IMO

> Personally, I'd prefer your suggestion above, doing static inference before dynamic inference, if possible.

That's only a partial solution though 🤔

There are ways to get the editor to assume a typed dict value for an untyped variable.
E.g.: (Untested but something like this)
```
var a: Dictionary[String, String] = {"a": "b"}
func test():
    var c = a
    for b in range(0, 1):
        c[b].
```
Would probably still error out.

> > I meant more from a Core perspective
> 
> Fair 👍, no clue what's going on internally, just saying the method behaves differently than I'd expect without documentation.
> 
> > It would be possible to check for `dictionary.get_key_type` before keying the dict
> 
> We only have a `Variant` and I'd rather not add special cases for different variant types there. If there is a unified Variant API to get something by key/index, there should be a unified way to test the validity of such a key/index IMO

That's certainly a possibility. I'd probably expect to be able to query the introspection of the method, check for the index type, and only call with the given key after confirming it's valid.

> > Personally, I'd prefer your suggestion above, doing static inference before dynamic inference, if possible.
> 
> That's only a partial solution though 🤔
> 
> There are ways to get the editor to assume a typed dict value for an untyped variable. E.g.: (Untested but something like this)
> 
> ```
> var a: Dictionary[String, String] = {"a": "b"}
> func test():
>     var c = a
>     for b in range(0, 1):
>         c[b].
> ```
> 
> Would probably still error out.

True. Personally, I wouldn't expect my IDE to suggest code in this case, but I can definitely see this is a nice QOL feature.
I think this possibility could still be caught by doing type inference for `c` - even though it wasn't explicitly set, we know it's the same as `a` in this example because it's effectively `const`. This is getting into deeper code analysis territory though for sure.

Not sure if I properly understood the discussion here. It's totally okay to actually grab the value out of dictionary and often preferred as it can be more specific than the static type. However, if the key is not a constant value, then it cannot just try to access it. Even if it is, there should be a check if the key exists first. So, there should not be any unsafe access during completion (a dictionary can have values of multiple types, so grabbing a random key is meaningless) . When it's not possible to get the actual value, then it falls back the static type.

> As for a quick fix for the blocker. Would be nice to know whether `Variant.has_key` is safe to use with invalid keys.

I tested it and indeed `has_key()` is **not** safe to check with invalid types. It's actually worse because it gives two errors.

I think that `get()` should definitely give some error but `has()` should just work. Even if it checks type first, just return `false` without an error.

All of this is also a symptom of the missing concept of "type" in the core, which could centralize all type checking. Without it we would have to implement once again a type-checking routine at this point for completion (which would be otherwise unnecessary). But this is a discussion for another day.
